text: Install Graft, see what it needs, and follow the five steps from setting up your Apple account to installing an app.

Download Graft.zip from GitHub Releases. Unzip it, move Graft.app to /Applications, and open it. Graft.app carries everything it needs: the graft CLI, with its own Python; cyan, zsign, ldid, ipatool, UnfairPlay and the other helpers. You don't need Homebrew, pipx, Python, Go, Xcode or libimobiledevice. The one exception is decrypting on a jailbroken device, which still needs libimobiledevice's iproxy and tools you install yourself (see Decrypt on a jailbroken device). Coming from Graft 1.x? See Upgrading from Graft 1.x.

A Mac with Apple silicon and macOS 14 or later. On an Intel Mac, Graft.app opens to a screen that says: "Graft 2.0 needs a Mac with Apple silicon. Graft 1.1 may work on an Intel Mac running macOS 15 or later, but it was never tested there." Graft 1.1 needs macOS 15; to install it, see Going back to 1.1, whose pipx command pins it with @v1.1. An iPhone or iPad paired with this Mac, connected by USB, or on the same network with Wi-Fi sync turned on. An Apple account, of one of two kinds. The first run asks which you have, and Settings switches later. A free Apple ID, with LiveContainer on the device. Graft builds unsigned IPAs and pushes them into LiveContainer, which signs them when you import them. Graft never signs anything itself on this account. A paid Apple Developer Program membership, with a development certificate exported as a .p12 and a provisioning profile (a wildcard profile is simplest) that includes your device.

To You need Build and push into LiveContainer LiveContainer on the device. With a free Apple ID, install it with SideStore, AltStore, iloader or Impactor, which also refresh it every 7 days. Install an app as a normal app (Sideload) A paid membership, its .p12 and a profile that includes the device. Install or update LiveContainer from Graft A paid membership and an App Store Connect API key. Make each app's provisioning profile automatically A paid membership and an App Store Connect API key. Search the App Store Nothing. No Apple ID is involved. Download from the App Store An Apple ID signed in in Graft. Any Apple ID works, free or paid; it's separate from the account above. The app must be one that Apple ID owns, or a free one Graft can get for it. Decrypt App Store downloads An iPhone or iPad app installed on this Mac from the Mac App Store, with the same Apple ID, and opened once. Any free one will do. Decrypt on a jailbroken device A jailbroken iPhone or iPad with frida-server 16.x and OpenSSH, plus tools you install yourself (see Decrypt on a jailbroken device). Run a build on this Mac PlayCover.
Each step has its own page: Set up your Apple account Add an app Give it a decrypted IPA Attach tweaks Build and install
Set Graft up for a free Apple ID or a paid Apple Developer account, and switch between the two later in Settings. The first time it opens, Graft asks "Do you have a paid Apple Developer account?"

No, I have a free Apple ID. That's all on the Mac. Graft lists the steps to do on the iPhone or iPad, with your free Apple ID: Install SideStore, or use iloader. Install LiveContainer (guide). The LiveContainer+SideStore build uses one app slot for both. In LiveContainer, open Settings and tap Import Certificate from SideStore, so it can sign the apps you import. iloader doesn't do this for you, and on iOS 26 every app fails its first launch with "JITLess mode is required since iOS 26" until it's done. Graft finds LiveContainer on the device by its bundle id, so there is no team id to set up.

Yes. Choose your .p12. Type its password (leave it empty if you set none). Choose your provisioning profile. Graft shows the team and the devices the profile covers before it sets anything up. It keeps the password in your login keychain, never in a file, and copies both files into its config folder.

The Account row in Settings switches between the two, with Add a paid account… or Switch to a free Apple ID…, and keeps your apps, repos and settings either way. With a paid account, Replace certificate and profile… swaps in a new pair when the old one expires, which happens every year.

Add an app to Graft from an App Store search, its App Store URL, or a name and bundle id, and see which App Store Graft looks it up in. Press + at the top of the sidebar. Add App opens on Search. Type an app's name, and pick it from the results. Choose its delivery, and press Add. You can also paste its App Store URL, or fill in a name and bundle id by hand.
Add App (+ at the top of the sidebar) has three ways in.

Search is the default. Type an app's name, and the App Store's iPhone apps that match appear as you type, each with its icon, developer and price. Results come from the store in the sheet's Store picker. It starts at this Mac's region (System Settings › General › Language & Region). A territory such as Puerto Rico or Réunion uses the store its people shop in (US, France), and a region with no App Store uses the US store and says so. Pick one with the mouse or the arrow keys, choose its delivery, and press Add (or Return). That adds it exactly as its App Store URL would. A paid app shows its price, and a listing that gives none says "Price unknown", never "Free". A result already in your config says so, and names the app it was added as. Apple's own apps can be found but not got: iOS ships them, and only Apple can sign them. Apple limits how often one Mac can search. A term you already searched while the sheet is open is answered from memory, and if Apple does say no, the sheet says to try again shortly.
Paste the app's apps.apple.com link.
A name and a bundle id, and optionally an IPA you already have.

section: Which store an app is looked up in
text: Graft remembers the store an app came from (store_country in config.yaml), and checks its updates, its icon and its price there. Edit App shows it under App Store and can change it. An app added from a URL keeps the store the URL names (apps.apple.com/gb/..., or the older itunes.apple.com/gb/...). An app with no store (one added in Graft 1.x, from a URL that names none, or by hand) is looked up in the store of this Mac's region, then in the US store, the one 1.x always asked. The first that sells it answers, and nothing is written. When neither has it, the error names both stores. A hand-written store_country that isn't an App Store is ignored, with a warning; UK is read as GB.

A build needs a decrypted IPA of the app. There are three ways to get one. From the App Store. Once you've signed in and set up decryption (see App Store Downloads), the app's Source IPA section has Get latest from App Store. Graft downloads the app, decrypts it on this Mac, and stages it. An IPA you already have. Drop it on the app's pane. A dump from your own jailbroken device, from the device's Decrypt card. See Decrypt on a jailbroken device. These are for personal use: your own Apple ID, apps you own or get for free, on your own devices. Don't redistribute decrypted or modified IPAs.

section: Other ways to get an IPA
text: A build needs a decrypted IPA of the app, staged in ~/.cache/graft/ipas/. Graft checks every Mach-O binary in it before injecting and warns if any is still encrypted; the build carries on, but the app will most likely not launch. With nothing staged, the build stops and lists the ways to get one. The App Store route has its own page, App Store Downloads.

Drop the IPA on the app's pane, or choose it in Add App's Manual mode. Graft checks that the IPA's bundle id matches the app's and stages it under its canonical name. An IPA that is still encrypted (straight from the App Store) is decrypted with UnfairPlay on the way in if decryption is set up, and refused if it isn't.

The device's Decrypt card dumps an installed app off your own jailbroken iPhone or iPad, and Add as app turns the dump into an app. This path needs tools Graft.app doesn't include, which you install yourself: Tool Used for frida 16.x on the device Both backends. The device's frida-server must be 16.x, the major frida-ios-dump's virtualenv installs. Graft has no frida of its own: it asks frida-ios-dump's (graft_ipa/frida_probe.py), so until frida-ios-dump is set up, the decrypt check can't reach frida-server and says so. frida-ios-dump One backend. Clone it to ~/.local/share/graft/frida-ios-dump, check out 56e99b2 (its last release for frida 16; the current one needs frida 17), and create a .venv there with pip install 'frida==16.*' paramiko scp tqdm, or set GRAFT_FRIDA_IOS_DUMP. The decrypt check prints these commands when it isn't set up. Needs OpenSSH on the device. bagbak The other backend. npm install -g bagbak@4.0.3 for a 16.x frida-server. iproxy, from libimobiledevice The SSH tunnel to the device. brew install libimobiledevice, or from MacPorts, sudo port install libimobiledevice. The card checks what, if anything, is blocking a dump right now. Unless you choose a backend, Graft picks the one that can run, preferring frida-ios-dump: frida-ios-dump attaches to the running app. Graft brings it to the foreground first, launching it if needed. It copies the bundle over SSH: store the device's root password with Set root password…, or set GRAFT_SSH_KEY (and GRAFT_SSH_USER if it isn't root). bagbak spawns the app itself. bagbak 4.x (the version that works with a 16.x frida-server) also copies the bundle over SSH, using the same stored root password; it can't use GRAFT_SSH_KEY. A dump is always of the whole app, which is what gets verified and staged. A dump that leaves app extensions encrypted (an extension built for a newer iOS than the device runs) drops them and stages the rest, and says what it removed. The app keeps working, minus those widgets and share extensions.

Cache lists every staged IPA, and marks the one a build uses when a bundle id has more than one. From there you can add a dump as an app, install it on this Mac with PlayCover, or delete it. Staged IPAs are never pruned.

Sign in and set up decryption once, and Graft downloads, decrypts and stages the apps your Apple ID owns or can get for free. Graft downloads the App Store's IPA with ipatool and decrypts it with UnfairPlay, both inside Graft.app. It only downloads apps your Apple ID already owns, or free ones it gets for that Apple ID; a paid app is bought in the App Store, never by Graft. Everything happens on your own Mac, for your own devices. There are two one-time steps, both in Settings › App Store: Sign in and Set up decryption. Settings is the last item in the sidebar, under Activity: Graft has no separate Settings window, so ⌘, opens nothing.

Press Sign In…. Type your Apple ID (email or phone) and password. Type the 6-digit code if Apple asks for one (it doesn't always). About signing in: Graft types your Apple ID, password and code into the bundled ipatool's own prompts. They go only to Apple, through that ipatool. Graft never saves them, and never puts them on a command line, in the environment or in a log. ipatool, which comes with Graft, keeps your sign-in, including your password, in your login Keychain, as it does when you use it on its own. The first App Store action on a Mac (usually the first sign-in) downloads ipatool's App Store components (about 320 MB, skipped if a 1.x ipatool already downloaded them) and its Unicorn emulator, and can take several minutes. Later ones take under a minute. See What Graft Downloads. If you signed in with your own ipatool under Graft 1, the sheet says so first: signing in here removes that sign-in, and your own ipatool will need to sign in again if you still use it in Terminal. See Upgrading from Graft 1.x. While you're signed in, Sign In Again… sits beside Sign Out. Use it when Apple has ended the session: a get then says so, and names the button. Sign Out signs ipatool out.

Install any free iPhone or iPad app from the Mac App Store (only an Apple silicon Mac can), signed in there with the same Apple ID you use in Graft, and open it once. Press Set Up Decryption…. In the sheet, pick that app (the first one is already picked) and press Set Up Decryption… again. Graft then explains what will happen; press Continue. macOS's dialog usually names Graft and asks you to allow it administrator access ("Allow administrator access for “Graft”?"). On a Mac with Touch ID it offers Touch ID or Use Password…; on one without, it asks for your password. If Graft has to start this step through osascript instead, the dialog names osascript. Cancel stops here. Graft never sees the password. If your macOS account isn't an administrator, macOS's dialog asks for an administrator's name and password instead, so someone who administers this Mac has to type them. The rest is the same: Graft never sees them, and the decryption model it sets up is yours. What happens: Graft explains the step before macOS's dialog appears, and shows the exact command under "The exact command, run as root". Root works only in a folder of its own, on its own copy of the app, and runs its own copy of UnfairPlay. In a Graft.app signed with a developer team, as releases are, root checks that copy against Graft.app's team before it runs it, and when Graft.app is signed with Developer ID, the copy must be too. A copy nothing can check is shown as a warning, and runs only if you press "Run Unchecked Copy as Root…". UnfairPlay saves a private decryption model, which Graft then moves into your own folder, as you. Cancel is always safe. The step also stops by itself if it runs far longer than expected (15 minutes for most apps, longer for a very large one). Decryption then works only for apps downloaded with that Apple ID. If you switch Apple ID, in Graft or in the Mac App Store, press Set Up Again… with an app installed under the new one.

On the app's pane, Get latest from App Store downloads, decrypts and stages the App Store's latest version. Stop cancels it and deletes the download. If your Apple ID doesn't have the app yet and it's free, the button becomes Get (free). Graft asks first, then adds the app to your Apple ID's purchases at no cost, as Get in the App Store would, and downloads it. A paid app shows Open in App Store instead. Buy it there, then get it in Graft. Add App's Search offers "Get it from the App Store after adding" once the App Store is set up.

The downloaded IPA carries your Apple ID and your license for the app. Graft keeps it in a private temporary directory, deletes it afterward, and runs UnfairPlay with --strip-account-data. It doesn't rely on that flag. Every IPA Graft stages, from any source, has iTunesMetadata.plist (your Apple ID and account ids) and every SC_Info/ license directory removed, and is checked for them before it goes into the cache. An IPA staged by an earlier version is cleaned the first time a build uses it, and so is anything a re-install or a Mac install hands over. If the cache can't be written (a full or read-only disk), the build warns and goes on from a cleaned copy instead. Only when no clean copy can be made does it stop, rather than ship the data. A sideload archive keeps the license files its signature seals, since removing them would break the install. Rebuild it to get rid of them. What gets staged, built and put on a device doesn't identify you.

UnfairPlay checks the decrypted pages against Apple's own hashes. If it can't (some older apps), Graft refuses the IPA and offers Use it anyway…, which says what that risks, then runs the same get or drop again. If such an app crashes at launch, the decrypt is the likely cause.

Find tweaks on Canister or in APT repositories, keep them in your tweaks library, and attach them to an app. Find tweaks under Canister or in your Repos. Download them into Tweaks. Press Attach… on the app's pane. A .deb or .dylib you already have goes into the tweaks folder too.

Canister searches canister.me. A download by package id is checked against Canister's published SHA-256, when Canister has one. Repos adds APT repositories and lists their packages. Free repositories only; repos that need a login or payment aren't supported. Tweaks lists your library (~/.config/graft/tweaks/), checks it for newer published versions when you ask, and updates a tweak, re-pointing the apps that use it. Deleting one an app still uses asks first, and offers Detach and Delete. Deleted tweaks go to the Trash.

cyan bundles ElleKit as CydiaSubstrate and adds a few common frameworks when a tweak links them, but not every shared library a tweak may link against (color or settings libraries, for example). If a build fails with Library not loaded: @rpath/libexample.dylib, put a sandbox-compatible copy of that library in the tweaks folder and attach it to the app, as you would a .deb.
Tweaks built for RootHide depend on libroothide.dylib, which doesn't exist outside a jailbreak. Use the rootless build from the developer's own repository or releases.

Build an app with its tweaks, push it into LiveContainer or, with a paid account, install it as a normal app, and keep track of past builds and deliveries. Press Build & Install. LiveContainer delivery: Graft pushes the IPA into LiveContainer's Documents. Open LiveContainer on the device and import it from there. That's when LiveContainer signs it and the tweaks start loading. Sideload delivery (paid only): Graft signs the IPA with your certificate and installs it as a normal app. Builds lists every build, with its log and archive. See Building.

Each app has a delivery mode, LiveContainer or Sideload. An app added without one is LiveContainer with a free Apple ID and Sideload with a paid account. Graft writes the mode whenever it adds an app, so an app keeps its mode if the config later changes account. Change it in the app's Edit sheet.

LiveContainer delivery builds the tweaked IPA unsigned and pushes it into LiveContainer's Documents folder over USB or Wi-Fi. You then import it inside LiveContainer, which runs it as a guest app. Why this is the main path: a guest app keeps its original bundle id, and some apps tie sign-in to their original bundle id. It also needs no provisioning profile of its own, so zsign, the profile and the device-in-profile checks are skipped for these builds. How a delivery works: Build & Install pushes Documents/<name>.ipa into LiveContainer. On the device, open LiveContainer. The IPA is in its Documents; import it as an app. LiveContainer signs it on import, and that is when the tweaks start loading. Optionally remove the pushed IPAs afterward, with Clean up in the device's LiveContainer section. Delivering is not installing: Graft can see what it put in Documents, not whether you imported it. See Delivery state.

Sideload delivery signs the IPA with zsign, using your .p12 and profile, and installs it on the device as a normal top-level app. The device's UDID must be in the profile. Use this for apps that don't care about their bundle id or signing team. On a free Apple ID, building, re-installing or adding a sideload app is refused.

Build & Install runs this pipeline. Build options (beside it) picks the device and can build without installing. Pre-flight. Tools, signing files, password, device, and that the device is in the profile. Only what the delivery mode needs is checked. Source IPA. The decrypted IPA staged in ~/.cache/graft/ipas/. Decryption check. The load commands of every Mach-O. Any that is still encrypted is reported as a warning naming the binary, and the build carries on. Inject. cyan, with the app's tweaks and options. The original bundle id is kept by default. cyan's output is meant to be re-signed: its modified binaries carry stale signatures until then. Every delivery re-signs before anything runs: zsign for Sideload, LiveContainer on import, SideStore or PlayCover on install. A LiveContainer build that isn't installed is for one of those signers. Sign (Sideload only). zsign with your .p12 and profile. Archive. Copy the result to ~/.cache/graft/built/. Deliver. Push into LiveContainer, or install on the device. Record. Write the build to ~/.local/state/graft/log.sqlite and apply archive retention. Stop ends the build where it is. A stopped build shows as Stopped, not as a failure, and adds no row to Builds.

Builds lists every build, with its saved log (View log…). A build's archive can be delivered again without rebuilding (Re-install…), or shown in Finder (Reveal in Finder). A re-install goes out the way the archive was built: an unsigned LiveContainer archive is never installed as a top-level app, and a zsign-signed one is never pushed into LiveContainer. If the app's delivery mode has changed since, rebuild it. For a build recorded before Graft 1.1 noted the mode, the archive itself says (zsign's embedded profile). After each successful build, all but the newest archive_keep archives per app version go to the Trash (default 2; 0 keeps only the build just made). Grouping by version means rebuilds of one version never push out the last build of an older version, so you can always roll back to a version you shipped. Builds you can re-install are kept first. An archive left by a build whose install failed only keeps a slot none of those needs. Archives go to the Trash, not straight to deletion, so the space comes back when you empty it. Staged source IPAs are never pruned. Clean up old builds… in Builds does the same at your archive_keep: it says how many archives would go to the Trash, and moves them when you confirm. Useful after lowering the setting. The button is disabled while a build runs. A clean-up never moves an archive that is still in use. A build holds a lock from the moment it archives its IPA until its history entry is written, and a re-install holds it until the archive is delivered. A Mac install copies a built archive under the lock and hands PlayCover the copy, since PlayCover reads the file after Graft has returned. A clean-up you start waits up to 30 seconds for them to finish, then stops with an error and moves nothing. A build's own clean-up doesn't wait: if another build is delivering, it skips this time and says so, and the next build catches up. Two clean-ups at once take turns.

The app list and each app's pane say whether building now would produce something different from what was last delivered. On every delivery Graft records a SHA-256 over what determines the build: the source IPA's bundle id and version, each tweak's filename and contents, the cyan options and the delivery mode. Comparing that with what the config would produce now gives one of: State Means never Nothing has been delivered for this app. stale Something changed since the last delivery; the reasons say what (for example some-tweak.deb rebuilt since delivery or app version changed: 1.2.3 → 1.3.0). current Matches the last delivery. unknown Graft can't tell (for example a tweak file it can't read, or no staged IPA), and says so instead of guessing. Tweak contents are hashed, not just names, because a tweak rebuilt from source keeps its filename. The source IPA is identified, not hashed. Limits worth knowing: Delivered is not installed. For LiveContainer, Graft knows it wrote the file, not whether you imported it. Checking the device lists LiveContainer's Documents and can only downgrade a state: a missing file means the record is out of date, but a present file doesn't prove an import. Checking the device leaves sideload apps alone. A re-install of an archive that a recorded push shipped, byte for byte (usually the newest build), is compared like that push. Any other re-installed archive reads stale, because what went into it wasn't recorded. None of this blocks a build.

On an Apple silicon Mac, an app's pane has Build for this Mac, which makes the build loadable under PlayCover and hands it to PlayCover. A staged IPA or an archived build can be handed over too. Some tweak libraries import iOS private frameworks that macOS doesn't have; for these Mac builds Graft bundles a minimal stand-in instead. Phone builds are never changed this way. Graft.app carries that stand-in prebuilt, so a Mac build needs no Xcode. A graft installed with pipx builds it on demand and needs full Xcode for that; see The CLI without the app.

Use the LiveContainer already on your device, or install and update one from Graft with a paid account, and see which LiveContainer a build pushes into. If LiveContainer is already on the device through SideStore, AltStore, iloader or Impactor, Graft uses it as it is. With a paid account Graft can also install and update LiveContainer itself, signed with your certificate so that guest apps keep their logins.

A device's pane has a LiveContainer section. It lists what is installed and who manages it, on either account. Install / Update LiveContainer and Put certificate on device are paid only. With a free Apple ID they're disabled, and the section points you at the store that installed LiveContainer. Clean up is there whenever the device has a LiveContainer, whoever installed it.

Up to three LiveContainers can be installed side by side, as com.kdt.livecontainer.<TEAM> (the primary), com.kdt.LiveContainer2.<TEAM> and com.kdt.LiveContainer3.<TEAM>. Every installer names them this way, with its team id, so Graft finds them on the device by bundle id: a ten-character team id after the name, whatever team it is, in any letter case. A free Apple ID needs no team id in the config. System apps count too, so a LiveContainer that TrollStore or a jailbreak installed (often as plain com.kdt.livecontainer) is found, and so is one an on-device re-signer gave some other suffix.

section: Which one a build pushes into
text: In this order: the app's pin (the LiveContainer picker in its Edit sheet, or lc_bundle_id: in config.yaml), in any letter case, or the id without its team suffix when that names exactly one. A pin that names nothing installed, or an app that isn't LiveContainer, stops the build with what was found; it's never quietly ignored; the only LiveContainer on the device, whatever its bundle id; with a paid account, the configured team's primary; the only primary (com.kdt.livecontainer.<TEAM>, or plain com.kdt.livecontainer). Anything else stops the build with a list of what was found. That includes plain com.kdt.livecontainer next to a com.kdt.livecontainer.<TEAM>: Graft can't tell which one you import from, so it asks you to pin one rather than guess. A build finds out before it injects anything: the push's target, and whether its <app>.ipa name is free there, are checked ahead of cyan. The sidebar names the LiveContainer a push would use, found the same way.

Installing LiveContainer needs an App Store Connect API key (Settings › App Store Connect) to fetch profiles. It also needs the App IDs above (plus the primary's extensions) registered at developer.apple.com with the App Groups capability and the group group.com.SideStore.SideStore.<TEAM> assigned. App groups can't be assigned through the API; if one is missing, the error names the App ID. On a device where AltStore or SideStore manages LiveContainer, Graft won't install over it, because replacing those copies would break every guest app signed through them. Update through AltStore or SideStore instead.

Put certificate on device is for a LiveContainer Graft installed: it has no AltStore to take a certificate from, and its JIT-less mode needs one. Import it in LiveContainer's Settings, then remove it with Remove certificate. Until then the certificate sits where guest apps can read it.

Graft never deletes or replaces a file in LiveContainer's Documents unless it knows the file is its own: a delivery record for that device and that LiveContainer, or, with no record (after a state reset, say), the file's SHA-256 matching one of that app's archived builds. Clean up removes only the IPAs Graft's deliveries recorded and a certificate it recorded pushing, and retires those records, so a file you later put there under the same name is yours. An AppleDevelopment.p12 with no record (one pushed by Graft 1.0, or your own) is reported and left in place. Putting the certificate on the device replaces it only when its bytes are your configured .p12. A build whose IPA name (<app>.ipa) is already taken by a file that isn't Graft's stops instead of overwriting it. Rename or remove that file in the Files app, then build again. A re-push of Graft's own earlier delivery replaces it as before.
Put the graft command on your Mac, either from Graft.app or with pipx. Graft in Terminal is optional; everything in the User Guide works without it.

In Graft.app, open Settings › Command-line tool and press Install graft for Terminal. It links the app's own graft into ~/.local/bin. If ~/.local/bin isn't on your shell's PATH, the section shows the line to add to your shell's startup file, with a Copy button. Open a new Terminal window afterward. The command runs the CLI inside the app, so it updates with the app, and Terminal and the app can't drift apart. If another graft is already in ~/.local/bin (a pipx install, say), the section says where it points and offers Replace it…. If a graft earlier on your PATH would win, it says that one is what Terminal runs. Move Graft.app to Applications first: the button won't link a copy running from a disk image or from where macOS put a downloaded app it moved aside.

To use Graft without the app, or to run it from source, install the CLI with pipx: pipx install git+https://github.com/GreenglassT/Graft # brew install pipx, if you need it pipx ensurepath pipx ensurepath adds ~/.local/bin to your PATH, so open a new terminal afterward for the graft command to be found. It needs Python 3.11 or later (the test suite passes on 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14). Graft.app never uses a pipx install. It always runs the copy inside it. To update it, run pipx reinstall graft-ipa. Once a new version is tagged on GitHub, pipx upgrade graft-ipa works too.

A pipx install doesn't include the tools Graft.app carries. Install the ones you use yourself: Tool Used for Install cyan (pyzule-rw) injecting tweaks pipx install --force https://github.com/asdfzxcvbn/pyzule-rw/archive/04a40f2aa65ec9cb36127f74d52ae4ef71377c50.zip (the commit tagged v1.4.4, the release Graft is tested with) zsign signing, for Sideload delivery (paid only) brew install zsign ipatool 2.8.0 App Store downloads graft --appstore-status prints the commands that download the release for your Mac's processor and put it at ~/.local/bin/ipatool. Use 2.8.0: 2.8.1 has a download bug, and Graft refuses it. UnfairPlay v0.4.0 decrypting App Store downloads, on Apple silicon A Go program, built from source to ~/.local/share/graft/unfairplay/unfairplay. graft --appstore-status prints the clone, checkout and go build commands. Full Xcode, selected (sudo xcode-select -s /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer) a PlayCover build whose tweak links an iOS private framework The stand-in framework is compiled with Xcode's iOS SDK, which the Command Line Tools don't have. Only such a build needs it, and only at that step; --check doesn't look for it. graft --check lists each missing tool with the command that installs it, and only the tools your apps' delivery modes use: zsign only when some app sideloads (or, on a paid config with no apps yet, since a new app sideloads by default). The brew commands need Homebrew, and --check says so when it isn't installed. Neither kind of install needs libimobiledevice or the Xcode Command Line Tools for phone builds: Graft reads binaries and installs apps itself, through pymobiledevice3.

cyan and zsign: Graft.app's own copy, then your PATH. config.yaml has no setting for either. ipatool and UnfairPlay: a path you set in config.yaml, then Graft.app's copy, then their usual install location, then your PATH (so a Homebrew ipatool is found too). Set them in an appstore: section (ipatool:, unfairplay:, unfairplay_models:), as full paths starting with / or ~/. A relative one is ignored, with a warning each time Graft runs, and read as not set. A path you set that points at nothing (you removed that ipatool, say): Graft.app, and the graft it links for Terminal, run their own copy instead, and --appstore-status notes the setting it passed over. Remove the key to stop the note. A pipx graft reports the tool as missing at that path. An appstore.ipatool of ~/.local/bin/ipatool, or an appstore.unfairplay of ~/.local/share/graft/unfairplay/unfairplay, is the 1.x default written out. It counts as not set, so Graft.app's copy still comes first. --appstore-status says so for ipatool, and marks the UnfairPlay that runs "(bundled)". To make your own ipatool win, put it somewhere else and set the path. Without unfairplay_models:, Graft uses UnfairPlay's own default: UNFAIRPLAY_MODEL_DIR if set, else ~/Library/Application Support/unfairplay/models. Setting up decryption in Graft.app always uses Graft.app's own UnfairPlay, because that step runs it as root. --check and --appstore-status say which copy they found, and mark Graft.app's own "(bundled)".

section: If --init couldn't read the team id
text: If --init couldn't read the team id from the profile, it writes team_id: REPLACEME. Set the real one with graft --set-settings --signing-team-id <TEAM> before --set-p12-password: the Keychain entry is keyed by team id, so --set-p12-password refuses until it's set. Instead of the Keychain, you can export the variable named by signing.cert_password_env. When that variable is set and not empty, builds use it rather than the Keychain's password, so unset it once you store a new password in the Keychain.

graft --init --account free and graft --init --account paid --p12 <file> --profile <file> do what answering the questions does, and are what the app runs. The paid one reads the .p12 password from stdin (one line), or asks for it without echo in Terminal, and makes the same checks as the app. Neither touches a config that doesn't parse. On a paid config, --account paid refuses unless given --replace (the app's Replace certificate and profile…), and --account free switches it to a free Apple ID (the app's Switch to a free Apple ID…): it removes the signing: section and keeps the apps, repos and settings. On a free config, --account paid adds the paid account (Add a paid account…). --dry-run checks everything and writes nothing. The interactive --init copies the files it's given as they are, so an expired profile shows up in --check, and a certificate the profile doesn't list only when the phone refuses the install. --config <path> works with any of these, for a config somewhere else. The app always uses the default one.
The graft commands, grouped by what they do. Almost every command takes --json (see Scripting), and every one takes --config <path>. graft --help lists every flag but --describe (see Scripting).

graft --list # apps: bundle id, pin, tweaks, delivery state, store (--json: account, mode) graft --appstore-search "example" # iPhone apps that match, from this Mac's region's store graft --appstore-search "example" --country GB --limit 10 graft --add-app https://apps.apple.com/app/id123456789 [--delivery livecontainer] graft --add-app-manual --name example --bundle-id com.example.app --display-name Example --store-country GB graft --remove-app example # cached IPAs and build history are kept --appstore-search needs no Apple ID. It asks the public iTunes Search API and sends only the search term and a country code. Its table ends with the --add-app-manual line for the store it searched: pass --store-country as it shows, so the app's update checks ask the same store. --country takes the two-letter code of a country with an App Store. A territory or UK is accepted as the store it uses (GB), with a note; a code with no store is refused. Without it, Graft uses the store of this Mac's region, or the US store if it can't read one or the region has none. --limit defaults to 25 and stops at 50. --json adds each result's icon, cached for a week in ~/.cache/graft/appstore-search-icons/.

To switch account in Terminal, run graft --init again: on a free config it offers to add a paid account, and on a paid one to switch to a free Apple ID, keeping apps, repos and settings either way.
Drive graft from a script with --json, and see which environment variables it reads, including the ones for running behind a proxy.

--json turns a command's output into newline-delimited JSON events on stdout. Every stdout line is one JSON object, and any command's narration and warnings go to stderr. This is how the Mac app talks to the CLI. Notices from before the command runs (a directory moved to its new name, an old environment variable still set) are log events with "source": "startup". --list starts with one account event, {"type":"account","account":"free"} or "paid", even when no apps are configured. The app events after it and the preflight-end event from --check carry the same account field. graft --describe prints the contract the app relies on: every flag and every event type. --help doesn't list it. A few commands don't answer in events. --init without --account refuses --json. --version, --setup-portal and the password prompts ignore it, and so do three whose output is fixed already: --build-log prints the saved log as it is (JSON Lines, since only builds run with --json save one), --describe always prints JSON, and --reveal-build prints nothing.

Variable Meaning the one named by signing.cert_password_env .p12 password: when set and not empty, used instead of the Keychain's GRAFT_SSH_USER, GRAFT_SSH_PASS, GRAFT_SSH_KEY SSH to a jailbroken device, for a dump GRAFT_FRIDA_IOS_DUMP where frida-ios-dump is cloned UNFAIRPLAY_MODEL_DIR UnfairPlay's own: where its model lives XDG_CONFIG_HOME, XDG_CACHE_HOME, XDG_STATE_HOME, XDG_DATA_HOME move Graft's directories HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, NO_PROXY (and the lower-case forms) send Graft's requests through a proxy REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, SSL_CERT_FILE, CURL_CA_BUNDLE, SSL_CERT_DIR trust another CA, such as a TLS-inspecting proxy's root Graft.app reads these from your login shell when it starts, and again when you press Check again (on the setup screen or beside Settings' PATH line) or Re-run in Preflight, at most once every 10 seconds. It runs the shell as an interactive login shell, given 5 seconds. csh and tcsh run as interactive shells, which read ~/.tcshrc or ~/.cshrc but not ~/.login. So a variable exported in ~/.zshrc or ~/.zprofile reaches the CLI it runs, as do your PATH additions and XDG_* directories. PYTHON* variables and the color switches (FORCE_COLOR, TTY_COMPATIBLE, TTY_INTERACTIVE, PY_COLORS, CLICOLOR_FORCE) are never passed on. If the shell doesn't answer, the app carries on without them (or, on a later Check again, with what it read before), and a startup file that hangs is stopped along with everything it started. On a Mac without the Xcode Command Line Tools, a startup file that runs one of their commands (git, say) can make macOS offer to install them when Graft starts, as opening a Terminal window would. Graft doesn't need them: cancel, or install them.

Graft's own requests (iTunes lookups, Canister, repos, LiveContainer's releases) honor the proxy variables. Graft.app's bundled Python trusts the CA certificates it ships (certifi) and /etc/ssl/cert.pem, never the macOS Keychain, so a proxy that re-signs TLS needs its root named in a CA variable: export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/path/to/corp-ca.pem (a PEM file holding the proxy's root, plus the public roots if you want the rest of the internet too). In Graft.app, and in the graft it links into ~/.local/bin, each of REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, SSL_CERT_FILE and CURL_CA_BUNDLE is used only when it names an existing, readable file by an absolute path, and SSL_CERT_DIR only when it names an existing folder. Otherwise it's ignored, so a stale export can't break every connection. OPENSSL_CONF and OPENSSL_ENGINES are always ignored there: they're meant for another OpenSSL. The pipx CLI passes all of these through untouched. ipatool and UnfairPlay are Go programs and use the macOS trust settings, Keychain included.

What config.yaml holds, and where Graft keeps its files. Settings holds what most people change: the default device, how many archives to keep, the signing files on a paid account, the App Store Connect key, the App Store sign-in, and the paths Graft uses. Each app's Edit sheet holds its options. Everything is stored in ~/.config/graft/config.yaml ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/graft if set), which you can also edit by hand. A configured app looks like this: signing: # paid only; leave it out for a free Apple ID cert: ~/.config/graft/AppleDevelopment.p12 cert_password_env: GRAFT_P12_PASS # when set, used instead of the Keychain's profile: ~/.config/graft/wildcard.mobileprovision team_id: ABCDE12345 cache_dir: ~/.cache/graft/ipas tweaks_dir: ~/.config/graft/tweaks archive_keep: 2 # archived builds kept per app version # default_device_udid: <UDID> apps: example: bundle_id: com.example.app preferred_version: latest delivery: livecontainer # or sideload store_country: "GB" # the App Store it's looked up in # lc_bundle_id: com.kdt.LiveContainer2.ABCDE12345 # pin a LiveContainer tweaks: - some-tweak.deb # files in tweaks_dir cyan: display_name: Example keep_bundle_id: true # some apps tie sign-in to their original bundle id strip_extensions: false strip_supported_devices: true compression_level: 6 The app re-reads your config each time its window comes back to the front, so a change made in an editor or in Terminal shows without a relaunch. If config.yaml doesn't parse, Settings says so at the top, shows the default paths and saves nothing until it's fixed. Fix it in an editor, and the notice clears when you come back to the window. Free or paid. A config with no signing: section (or an empty one) is a free Apple ID. signing: keys that end up at the top level (lost indentation) are an error naming them, not a free config. Add a paid account… asks only for the .p12 and the profile, then adds a signing: section to the config and keeps its apps, repos and settings. With a paid account an app with no delivery mode is a sideload app, so Graft writes LiveContainer delivery into each such app and says which. Nothing moves until you change one. Switch to a free Apple ID… removes the signing: section and keeps everything else. Apps with no delivery mode then go into LiveContainer. One set to Sideload stays set, and won't build until you switch it to LiveContainer. Replace certificate and profile… swaps in a new pair, its Keychain password and the signing: section, keeps everything else, and puts the old ones back if any step fails. When the new pair belongs to another team, the old team's Keychain password is removed. The paid setup checks that the .p12 opens with its password and that the profile lists its certificate and hasn't expired. It copies both files into the config folder (0600, never through a link). Bundle id. Some apps tie sign-in to their original bundle id; keep_bundle_id: true (the default) preserves it. With keep_bundle_id: false cyan renames it (to new_bundle_id, or the original plus .plus) in both delivery modes, LiveContainer included. Renaming the bundle id also removes any Apple Watch app, which can't install under a new id. Per-app profiles (paid only). "Create the provisioning profile automatically" in an app's Edit sheet (auto_profile: true) has Graft create and cache a profile for the app through the App Store Connect API; profile: <path> points one app at a specific profile. Both apply to sideload builds only, and the option is locked on a LiveContainer app, which uses no profile. Make an API key at App Store Connect, then give it to Graft in Settings › App Store Connect. Graft checks the key by listing your devices, and only then copies the .p8 beside config.yaml. Setting a key replaces only the key and its devices. A profile_cache_dir you set by hand stays, and device_udids is refreshed every time with every enabled iPhone, iPad and iPod touch App Store Connect lists. To keep a list you curated, add device_udids_pinned: true to the app_store_connect: section. The lock file. Graft takes a lock on config.yaml.lock beside the config while it edits it, so the app and the CLI never write over each other. If you keep the config in a dotfiles repository and symlink it, add config.yaml.lock to that repository's .gitignore.

~/.config/graft/ ├── config.yaml ├── config.yaml.lock ├── AppleDevelopment.p12 ├── wildcard.mobileprovision ├── AuthKey_<KEY_ID>.p8 # App Store Connect API key ├── profiles/ # profiles made through that API └── tweaks/ # .deb and .dylib files ~/.cache/graft/ ├── ipas/ # staged decrypted IPAs (never pruned) ├── built/ # archived builds (newest archive_keep per app version) └── artwork/ # cached app icons ~/.local/state/graft/ ├── log.sqlite # build history and delivery records ├── build-logs/ # saved event log of each --json build (so every build from the app) ├── repos/ # cached APT repository indexes └── tweak-rollback/ # previous versions kept when a tweak is updated ~/.local/share/graft/ # tools you install for Graft (frida-ios-dump; UnfairPlay, for a pipx install) These four graft directories are owner-only (0700): Graft creates them that way and tightens them on every run if they aren't. Staged IPAs, archived builds, build logs and the .p12 and profile the setup copies are written 0600. Graft changes nothing outside these directories, and leaves alone a graft that is a symlink you made. Outside them, the App Store tools keep their own files: ipatool's sign-in in your login keychain and its downloads in ~/Library/Caches/ipatool, and UnfairPlay's model in ~/Library/Application Support/unfairplay/models.

When Graft goes online and what it downloads, including the one-time downloads on the first App Store action. Graft has no telemetry, analytics, crash reporting or update check, and it doesn't update itself. Graft.app makes no connections of its own: its CLI does, for something you asked for or a pane you opened, and to look up the icon of an app that has none yet, at launch and when the app list changes. Device UDIDs never leave your Mac. When Who it contacts What for You search the App Store, add an app, or open an app's pane; for an app with no icon yet, at launch, when the app list changes, and after a build or App Store get Apple's iTunes lookup and search, and its artwork CDN The app's version, price and icon You search, fetch or update tweaks canister.me, and the repos you add Tweak listings and downloads A device's pane opens, Edit App opens for a LiveContainer app, or you install LiveContainer GitHub LiveContainer's releases A paid account with an App Store Connect key makes a profile Apple's App Store Connect API Provisioning profiles You sign in, get an app, or get a free one Apple's App Store, through the bundled ipatool Your sign-in, the license, the IPA The first App Store action on a Mac (usually the first sign-in) PyPI (files.pythonhosted.org), and Apple's software CDN ipatool's Unicorn emulator (a few MB) and its App Store components (about 320 MB, skipped if a 1.x ipatool already downloaded them), once About that first App Store action: Graft.app doesn't include Unicorn. The bundled ipatool downloads Unicorn 2.1.4 from PyPI on first use, as upstream ipatool does, and checks it against the SHA-256 its source pins. Both downloads are cached in ~/Library/Caches/ipatool, so they happen once, and again only for a new version. Offline, that first App Store action stops with "ipatool needs to download its App Store emulator (Unicorn, from PyPI) the first time; connect to the internet and try again." UnfairPlay has no network code, and talking to your iPhone or iPad stays on your Mac and your local network. What Graft connects to lists every host, when, and what is sent.

Every host that Graft.app, the graft CLI, or a tool bundled in the app contacts: why, when, and what it sends. It was gathered by reading the code (graft_ipa/, Graft/Graft/, the bundled Python packages), the pinned sources of ipatool 2.8.0 and UnfairPlay 0.4.0, and the bundled binaries' strings. It covers Graft 2.0. Short version: Graft has no telemetry, analytics, crash reporting or update check. It doesn't update itself. The app makes no connections of its own. Everything goes through the CLI and the tools it runs. Your Apple ID, your password and the 2FA code, if Apple asks for one, go only to Apple, through the bundled ipatool. You type them into Graft's sign-in sheet (Settings › App Store › Sign In…), or graft --appstore-login asks for them in Terminal. Graft passes them over stdin to ipatool's own prompts and never stores them. ipatool keeps the sign-in, including the password, in your login keychain. The first App Store action on a Mac (usually the first sign-in) downloads ipatool's Unicorn emulator from PyPI and about 320 MB of App Store components from Apple, once. The components are skipped if a 1.x ipatool already downloaded them. Device UDIDs never leave your Mac.

The CLI sends User-Agent: graft/<version> (+https://github.com/GreenglassT/Graft) with every request it makes through requests. The exception is downloading icon images (--artwork, and the icons of --appstore-search results), which send the library's default User-Agent. Bold marks user data. Host Contacted by When What's sent itunes.apple.com (/lookup) CLI: --add-app, --appstore-check, --artwork, and the free-price check before --appstore-claim --add-app: when you add an app. The app also runs the other two on its own: --appstore-check when an app's detail pane opens; --artwork at launch, when the app list changes, and after a build or App Store get, but only for apps with no icon cached or in a cached IPA. The price check: when a get is refused for want of a license, and before Get (free). The App Store id from the URL you gave, or the app's bundle id, and the two-letter store the app came from (the one Search asked, or the one its URL names; else this Mac's region's store, then the US store if that one doesn't sell it). No account. itunes.apple.com (/search) CLI: --appstore-search When you type in Add App › Search: once you pause for half a second, for 2 or more characters, and only for a term not already searched in that sheet. Never on its own. The search term, and a two-letter country code (the sheet's Store picker, which starts at this Mac's region; or --country). No account. Apple's artwork CDN (whatever image URL the lookup returns) CLI: --artwork, --appstore-search After a lookup that found an icon; and for each search result's small icon not already cached (kept a week) The request only api.canister.me CLI: --search (Canister), --fetch <package id>, --tweak-updates (the Tweaks update check), --update-tweak When you search, fetch or check for tweak updates. The app never checks for tweak updates on its own. Redirects are followed. The request only api.appstoreconnect.apple.com CLI, paid accounts only: Settings › App Store Connect (--set-portal), --setup-portal, a sideload build with automatic provisioning, paid --lc-install During setup, and when a build has to create or refresh a provisioning profile An ES256 JWT signed with your App Store Connect API key (.p8), naming its issuer and key id; bundle ids (or wildcard patterns) and profile names. Graft reads the team's device list and matches UDIDs on the Mac; it never uploads one. github.com, api.github.com, and release-assets.githubusercontent.com, where GitHub redirects the release files (the LiveContainer project's) CLI: --lc-status, --lc-install --lc-status runs on its own when a device's pane opens, and in Edit App for a LiveContainer app. --lc-install runs when you install LiveContainer. The request only

Graft runs ipatool 2.8.0 for everything that needs your Apple ID. ipatool 2.8 runs every App Store request through an emulator that runs Apple's own Store framework on Unicorn. Its source pins every host it signs in to and talks to with your session: an authenticated request goes only to apple.com, *.apple.com, *.mzstatic.com or *.cdn-apple.com (internal/store/emulator/client.go). A download goes to whatever URL Apple's answer names. What When Hosts What's sent Sign in (--appstore-login, which runs ipatool auth login) When you press Sign In… in Settings › App Store, or run graft --appstore-login. Never on its own. Offline, that first action fails with "ipatool needs to download its App Store emulator (Unicorn, from PyPI) the first time; connect to the internet and try again." Over USB or the local network, never the internet. ipatool 2.8.0: as above. It is built from its pinned source, unpatched, and its only entitlements are allow-jit and disable-library-validation, which its emulator needs. UnfairPlay 0.4.0: no network code. It is built from its pinned source, unpatched, with no entitlements. Its Go build info lists only cobra, pflag and a plist library, with cgo off, and it imports no socket calls. Graft runs unfairplay --version and unfairplay decrypt, and Set Up Decryption runs unfairplay setup as root, offline. zsign 1.1.3: offline as Graft runs it (-k -p -m -o). It has an OCSP certificate check behind -C/--check, which Graft never passes. cyan and its helpers (ldid, insert_dylib, lipo, install_name_tool, otool): no network code. pymobiledevice3: everything Graft calls is local, through usbmuxd: device listing and lockdown values; InstallationProxy, AFC, HouseArrest and SpringBoardServices. The library's own network code isn't on any path Graft calls: personalization (TSS to gs.apple.com), developer disk image downloads, restore, activation and tunnels. Graft never mounts a developer image. frida: not bundled. Graft asks frida-ios-dump's own frida (graft_ipa/frida_probe.py) about local and USB devices only. Graft never uses remote frida. Python and the other packages: nothing connects on import, and nothing checks for updates.

Graft.app has no networking code: no URLSession, web views or remote images. It runs the bundled CLI, and the rows above are those CLI runs. Search results' icons, too, are downloaded by the CLI and drawn from its cache. It opens these only when you click them, in your browser or in the app that handles them: App Store Connect's API keys page, from Settings › App Store Connect; the upgrade guide's "Going back to 1.1" section on GitHub, from How to install Graft 1.1 on the screen an Intel Mac shows; Graft's releases page on GitHub (github.com/GreenglassT/Graft/releases), from the link under the license notice in Graft › About Graft; the guides the free-account setup's device steps link, each from its Open button: sidestore.io, iloader on github.com, and LiveContainer's installation guide on livecontainer.github.io; an app's apps.apple.com page, from Open in App Store on an app's pane, or the Mac App Store when Graft has no page for the app; the Mac App Store, from Open the Mac App Store in Set Up Decryption. Help › Licenses opens a folder inside the app. Other URLs in Graft, such as install hints, only appear as text you can copy. Graft never fetches any of these pages.

How to move to a new version of Graft.app. Download the new Graft.zip from GitHub Releases and replace the Graft.app in /Applications. Graft doesn't update itself. Your config, apps and builds carry over, and so does your App Store sign-in from 2.0 on. From 1.x, you sign in once. The Terminal command points into the app, so it updates too. From Graft 1.x, read Upgrading from Graft 1.x first: what happens to your config, your pipx graft, your Homebrew tools and your App Store sign-in, and how to go back to 1.1.

Graft 2.0 carries its own CLI and tools inside Graft.app, and does setup, App Store sign-in and decryption set-up in the app. Your config, apps, tweaks, staged IPAs and build history carry over as they are. This page covers what changes for someone coming from 1.0 or 1.1, and how to go back. The short version: Check your Mac: 2.0 needs macOS 14 or later. Graft 2.0 needs a Mac with Apple silicon. Graft 1.1 may work on an Intel Mac running macOS 15 or later, but it was never tested there. Replace Graft.app in /Applications with 2.0's, and open it. Settings › App Store › Sign In… once. It replaces the sign-in your own ipatool made under 1.x. Optional: remove the pipx graft, then Settings › Command-line tool › Install graft for Terminal. Optional: remove the Homebrew tools 2.0 no longer uses.

2.0 uses the same folders as 1.x: ~/.config/graft, ~/.cache/graft, ~/.local/state/graft and ~/.local/share/graft. It reads your config.yaml as it is, and doesn't rewrite it when it starts. Because a config exists, the first-run setup is skipped and the app opens on your apps. Most settings mean what they meant in 1.x. These are the differences. appstore.ipatool and appstore.unfairplay. 2.0 runs the ipatool and UnfairPlay inside Graft.app unless you chose another copy. A value equal to 1.x's default counts as not set: ~/.local/bin/ipatool for ipatool, ~/.local/share/graft/unfairplay/unfairplay for UnfairPlay. Graft.app's own copies run instead. For ipatool, graft --appstore-status says so; for UnfairPlay, it marks the copy that runs "(bundled)". A path that isn't there any more, because you removed that ipatool or UnfairPlay as Tools you no longer need allows, doesn't count either: Graft.app runs its own copy, and graft --appstore-status notes the setting it passed over. Remove the key from config.yaml to stop the note. Any other full path that is there still wins, for downloads and decrypts alike. To keep using your own ipatool, put it somewhere other than ~/.local/bin/ipatool and set appstore.ipatool to that path. Signing in with it in Graft first deletes the sign-in Graft.app's own ipatool made, so going back to that one means signing in again. A sign-in another ipatool made is saved over instead, and macOS may ask for your login keychain password while it is. Setting up decryption in Graft.app always uses Graft.app's own UnfairPlay, whatever the config says, because that step runs it as root. A relative path (one that doesn't start with / or ~/) is now ignored: the config still loads, each run warns that the setting isn't a full path, and Graft reads it as not set. Graft.app then runs its own copy, and a pipx graft looks in the usual places. 1.x resolved it against whatever folder the CLI started in. Fix the path, or remove it, to stop the warning. appstore.unfairplay_models works as before, but for the same rule: a relative path is ignored with a warning, and the default models folder is used. cyan and zsign. config.yaml never had a setting for either. 2.0 runs Graft.app's own copies, so the ones you installed with pipx and Homebrew are no longer used by the app. Apps added in 1.x have no store_country. 2.0 records the App Store an app came from, and looks it up there. An app with none is now looked up in the store of this Mac's region first, then in the US store, which is the only one 1.x asked. See App Store lookups. app_store_connect:. Setting a key in 2.0 replaces only the key and its device list. A profile_cache_dir you set by hand stays, and the list holds every enabled iPhone, iPad and iPod touch, not the first three. To keep a list you curated, add device_udids_pinned: true to the section. New keys. 2.0 may write store_country on an app. It reads device_udids_pinned in app_store_connect:, which only you add, and keeps it when it writes that section. 1.1 ignores both and keeps them when it edits the config. Passwords in the Keychain. Your .p12 password and your device's SSH password stay where 1.x stored them, and 2.0 reads them without asking. One 1.1 bug is fixed: storing a password again over one already there asked for your login keychain password, and replaced it even when you canceled. 2.0 doesn't ask.

Graft.app 2.0 never runs a pipx graft. It always runs the copy inside it. You can keep the pipx one for Terminal, or replace it. To replace it with the app's own: pipx uninstall graft-ipa Then, in Graft.app, Settings › Command-line tool › Install graft for Terminal. That links the app's graft into ~/.local/bin, where pipx kept its own, and the command then updates with the app. If you'd rather keep the pipx install around, the same section offers Replace it… instead, which repoints ~/.local/bin/graft at the app and leaves the pipx copy installed. If you keep it, both read and write the same config and files. Terminal runs whichever graft comes first on your PATH. Settings › Command-line tool says which one that is. A 1.1 graft asks every app's version and icon in the US store only. 1.1's graft --setup-portal rewrites the whole app_store_connect: section: it keeps only the first three enabled devices, and drops device_udids_pinned and a profile_cache_dir you set by hand. 1.1's App Store commands run your own ipatool, which can't read the sign-in Graft.app makes without a Keychain dialog. See Your App Store sign-in. pipx reinstall graft-ipa brings a pipx install up to 2.0, unless you pinned it to @v1.1 to go back (see Coming back to 2.0). It's still a separate copy: it runs the tools on your PATH and your own ipatool, never Graft.app's.

Graft.app 2.0 brings its own copy of each tool it uses, or does the job itself. None of these is needed for anything the app does: 1.x needed For 2.0 Python 3.11+ and pipx the CLI Graft.app carries its own Python and CLI. Going back to 1.1 needs them again. cyan, installed with pipx injecting tweaks bundled zsign, from Homebrew Sideload signing bundled ideviceinstaller and idevice_id, from libimobiledevice installing and finding devices done through pymobiledevice3, inside the CLI otool, from the Xcode Command Line Tools checking an IPA is decrypted done by Graft's own Mach-O reader ipatool 2.8.0 at ~/.local/bin/ipatool App Store downloads bundled UnfairPlay, built with Go into ~/.local/share/graft/unfairplay/ decrypting App Store downloads bundled full Xcode a PlayCover build whose tweak links an iOS private framework Graft.app carries the stand-in framework prebuilt You can remove them if nothing else of yours uses them, for example pipx uninstall cyan, brew uninstall zsign ideviceinstaller, and ~/.local/share/graft/unfairplay/. Keep them if you keep a pipx graft, which still needs them. Before removing your own ipatool, read Your App Store sign-in: it's what holds your 1.x sign-in. What 2.0 still uses, if you use it: decrypting on a jailbroken device still needs tools you install yourself. iproxy, from libimobiledevice (brew install libimobiledevice), for the SSH tunnel to the device. So if you dump apps from a jailbroken device, keep libimobiledevice. frida-ios-dump, with its own virtualenv and frida 16, and bagbak, as in 1.x. The 2.0 CLI has no frida of its own; it asks frida-ios-dump's. So if you used only bagbak, set frida-ios-dump up too: without it, Decrypt the app on screen (--decrypt-frontmost) doesn't work, and the decrypt check can't reach frida-server. PlayCover, to run builds on this Mac.

What 1.x left. Under 1.x you signed in with your own ipatool in Terminal (ipatool auth login). ipatool keeps that sign-in in your login keychain as three items under the service ipatool-auth.service: account, anisette-v4 and kbsync-v1. macOS lets only the program that made an item read it without asking, and Graft.app's ipatool is a different program from yours. Before you sign in. Settings › App Store reads "signed in by another ipatool (Graft 1's?): sign in again". Graft looks only at whether the items are there, never inside them, so opening Settings shows no Keychain dialog. Get latest from App Store refuses until you sign in, and says why. Signing in. Press Sign In…. The sheet says what will happen: "This also signs out any ipatool you installed yourself; it will need to sign in again if you use it in Terminal." Graft deletes those three items, by their exact service and account name, and nothing else. Deleting them shows no dialog. Graft's ipatool then signs in. Your Apple ID and password, and the code if Apple asks for one, are typed into its prompts and go only to Apple, through that ipatool. Graft saves none of them. ipatool keeps the new sign-in, password included, in your login keychain, and reads it from then on without asking, across Graft updates too. If your login keychain is locked, or doesn't answer, Graft says it couldn't check it and doesn't sign in. Unlock it in Keychain Access and try again. The first App Store action on a Mac (usually the first sign-in) downloads ipatool's App Store components (about 320 MB, skipped if a 1.x ipatool already downloaded them) and its Unicorn emulator (a few MB), once. See What Graft connects to. Your own ipatool afterward. In Terminal, it's signed out. If you run it, macOS shows two Keychain dialogs about the items Graft's ipatool made, because they aren't its own: "ipatool wants to use your confidential information stored in “ipatool-auth.service”…" and "ipatool wants to access key “ipatool-auth.service”…". Both ask for your login keychain password, even to Allow. If you Deny them, your ipatool prints "…could not be found in the keyring", and Graft.app stays signed in. Signing your ipatool in over those items can ask for the password too. If you don't need your own ipatool any more, leave it signed out. 2.0 test builds. If you signed in with a 2.0 test build, sign in once more. Their record of which items Graft's ipatool made is in an older format, which 2.0 doesn't trust, so Settings reads "signed in by another ipatool".

1.x set up decryption in Terminal, with sudo unfairplay setup --app "/Applications/<app>.app". 2.0 does it in Settings › App Store › Set Up Decryption…, behind macOS's administrator prompt. See Set up decryption. If you set up decryption in 1.x, you don't need to again. Both versions run UnfairPlay 0.4.0 and keep its model in the same place (~/Library/Application Support/unfairplay/models). Settings › App Store shows UnfairPlay as enrolled, as long as the model is yours: a model or folder another user owns, such as root, is reported with what to do. Setting up again on the same Mac with the same Apple ID makes the same model, byte for byte, so there's nothing to gain from it. The Apple ID must match. The model only decrypts apps downloaded with the Apple ID that installed the Mac App Store app it came from. Use the same Apple ID in Graft as in the Mac App Store. If you sign in to Graft with a different Apple ID from the one you used in 1.x, press Set Up Again… with an app installed under the new one. Older models stay beside the new one.

Every lookup of an app now goes through one rule: the update check, its icon, and the price Get (free) checks. An app with a store_country is looked up in that store only. An app with none is looked up in the store of this Mac's region (System Settings › General › Language & Region), then in the US store. The first store that sells it answers, for that lookup only; nothing is written to the config. When neither has it, the error names both. Apps added in 1.x have no store_country, so: On a Mac whose region uses the US store, or whose region Graft can't read, nothing changes. Elsewhere, an app your region's store sells is now checked there, so its version, price and icon come from that store. An app only the US store sells is still found, in the US store. To pin an app to one store, set App Store in its Edit sheet, or run graft --set-app-options --app <name> --store-country US.

Graft 1.1 needs macOS 15 or later: its app doesn't open on macOS 14. Graft 2.0 needs a Mac with Apple silicon. Graft 1.1 may work on an Intel Mac running macOS 15 or later, but it was never tested there. Graft 1.1 stays available: the app: Graft.zip on the v1.1 release; its CLI, which the 1.1 app runs for everything. It needs Python 3.11 or later and pipx, which 2.0 let you remove. Homebrew's pipx brings a Python with it: brew install pipx # if you removed it, or never had it pipx ensurepath # then open a new Terminal window pipx install --force "git+https://github.com/GreenglassT/Graft@v1.1" Keep the @v1.1. The 1.1 app's own setup screen and its release page say pipx install git+https://github.com/GreenglassT/Graft, with no tag: since 2.0, that installs 2.0's CLI, which the 1.1 app was never tested with. the tools it needs (cyan, zsign, libimobiledevice and ideviceinstaller, the Xcode Command Line Tools, and for App Store downloads ipatool 2.8.0 and UnfairPlay), which its own README lists. Replace Graft.app in /Applications with 1.1's. The 1.1 app looks for graft in ~/.local/bin first. If you installed graft for Terminal from 2.0, its link was there, and the --force in the install command above has already replaced it with the 1.1 CLI's, so there's nothing to remove. Staying on 1.1. If you never moved to 2.0 and installed 1.1's CLI as its own README says, with no tag, pipx upgrade graft-ipa and pipx reinstall graft-ipa now bring 2.0's CLI in under your 1.1 app. Run the pipx install --force …@v1.1 command above before either: pipx then keeps the 1.1 CLI (see Coming back to 2.0). What 1.1 makes of 2.0's state: 2.0 left 1.1 config.yaml Loads and edits it. It ignores store_country and device_udids_pinned, keeps them when it writes, and asks every app's version in the US store. Its --setup-portal rewrites app_store_connect: as above. A config that 2.0 wrote is otherwise one 1.1 understands. Staged IPAs, archived builds, tweaks, repos and log.sqlite Uses them as they are. The decryption model Uses it as it is: same UnfairPlay version, same folder. The sign-in record, ~/.local/state/graft/appstore-signin.json Doesn't know it, and ignores it. The App Store sign-in 2.0's ipatool made Can't read it without asking. 1.1 runs your own ipatool, so macOS shows two Keychain dialogs when it reads those items, in Settings › App Store and on a get, each asking for your login keychain password (see Your own ipatool afterward), and signing your ipatool in over them can ask for it too. To give 1.1 a clean start with the App Store, delete those items first, then sign your own ipatool in as 1.1 says: security delete-generic-password -s ipatool-auth.service -a account security delete-generic-password -s ipatool-auth.service -a anisette-v4 security delete-generic-password -s ipatool-auth.service -a kbsync-v1

Graft.app 2.0 reads "signed in by another ipatool" again, and Sign In… replaces that sign-in as described above. pipx remembers the @v1.1, so pipx reinstall graft-ipa and pipx upgrade graft-ipa keep the 1.1 CLI. To un-pin it, either remove it and use the app's own: pipx uninstall graft-ipa then Settings › Command-line tool › Install graft for Terminal; or, to keep a pipx CLI of 2.0, install it again without the tag: pipx install --force git+https://github.com/GreenglassT/Graft

A guest app in LiveContainer doesn't remember its login LiveContainer was signed with a wildcard profile's entitlements (for example by zsign). Reinstall it from Graft with a paid account. Usually the frida majors differ, SSH to the device is down, or the app couldn't be brought to the foreground. no LiveContainer found on the device LiveContainer isn't installed, or not under a bundle id starting com.kdt.livecontainer. With a free Apple ID, install it through SideStore or iloader; see Set up your Apple account. With a paid account, Graft can install it too. the device listed no apps at all, which is how a locked phone answers The phone is locked, or hasn't been unlocked since it restarted. Unlock it, stay on the home screen, and try again. ... already has a Documents/<app>.ipa that Graft did not push LiveContainer's Documents already holds a file with the name the push uses, and neither a record nor its bytes say Graft put it there (it may be your own copy). Rename or remove it in the Files app (On My iPhone > LiveContainer), then build again. lc_bundle_id ... is not installed The app is pinned to a LiveContainer that isn't on the device. Pick one in the LiveContainer picker in the app's Edit sheet, or Automatic to drop the pin. couldn't reach usbmuxd macOS's service for talking to iPhones didn't answer. Reconnect the phone; if it persists, restart the Mac. N LiveContainers are installed and Graft will not guess which to use There is no single primary: two LiveContainers installed by two Apple IDs, say, or a jailbreak's plain com.kdt.livecontainer next to an installer's com.kdt.livecontainer.<TEAMID>. Pin the app to one of the ids the error lists, in the LiveContainer picker in its Edit sheet. ... needs a paid Apple Developer Program membership The config has no signing: section, so it is set up for a free Apple ID, and the action needs a paid one. Use LiveContainer delivery, or, with a paid membership, Settings › Add a paid account…; it keeps your apps. Settings › App Store says "signed in by another ipatool (Graft 1's?): sign in again", or, with your own ipatool set in config.yaml, "a sign-in this ipatool can't read (another ipatool's?): sign in again" Your sign-in was made by an ipatool this one can't read: with Graft's own, such as yours under Graft 1; with your own, Graft.app's or another. Press Sign In…; see Upgrading from Graft 1.x. A decrypt fails as the wrong model or the wrong Apple ID Decryption was set up with another Apple ID. Use the same Apple ID in Graft as in the Mac App Store, then press Set Up Again… in Settings › App Store. Set Up Decryption… or Set Up Again… stops with "canonical input has no SIDB state" This Mac's App Store state, which UnfairPlay reads, isn't there right now: macOS sometimes clears it, even for an app you've already opened. Open the app you picked once, then set up again. The sheet says the same. The first sign-in, or the first App Store action, fails while it downloads ipatool's App Store components, with an error naming the macOS 27.0.1 (26A434) restore image (for example "server returned 404 Not Found") A known issue in 2.0. The bundled ipatool takes the App Store's frameworks from one macOS restore image, at a fixed Apple address, and if Apple removes that file, a Mac that hasn't downloaded them yet can't get them. A Mac whose ipatool already did (in ~/Library/Caches/ipatool, a 1.x ipatool's included) isn't affected. How to build Graft.app and run its tests from the repository. brew install xcodegen cd Graft && xcodegen generate open Graft.xcodeproj Or from the command line: xcodebuild -project Graft/Graft.xcodeproj -scheme Graft -configuration Debug \ -destination 'platform=macOS' build Build Debug: it runs the graft it finds on your PATH, and its setup screen first shows the commands that install the CLI, each with a Copy button. Release builds come from scripts/graft-release, below. A plain Xcode Release build has no CLI inside it, so it opens on a screen saying so. Tests: python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[dev]' .venv/bin/python -m pytest cd Graft && TEST_RUNNER_PATH="$PWD/../.venv/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin" \ xcodebuild test -scheme Graft -destination 'platform=macOS' The app is SwiftUI. It runs the graft CLI as a subprocess for every action and reads its --json events. Both share config.yaml and log.sqlite, and there's no daemon. A release build carries the CLI and its own Python inside the app. A build from Xcode runs the CLI it finds on your PATH, such as the repo's venv. scripts/graft-release builds the distributable app: everything bundled (arm64, with a universal app executable that shows Intel Macs a "needs Apple silicon" screen), signed with a Developer ID identity and zipped. Then scripts/verify-bundle checks the sealed app. See Graft/README.md, and docs/network.md for every host Graft and its tools contact, including what a release build downloads.
